title.en: Mountain Uncle and the Looking-Glass Trap

region.zh: 江原道山野（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Fairy tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Unmannerly Tiger', eBook #67180

summary.en: 'Mountain Uncle' is the splendid striped tiger of the Kang-wen highlands, who boasts he has never been wounded and laughs at traps. Coming round a great rock he sees a big tiger like himself and leaps to fight it — into a pit under a lid of logs, for the hunter had hung a looking-glass on the upright timbers, and the tiger, not seeing any water, was deceived into thinking a real tiger wanted to fight him. A kindly Buddhist priest opens the trap; the freed tiger thanks him and announces he must eat him up. The spirit in the tree and the spirit in the rock both judge against him, the rock warning that the Mountain Spirit, who rides on the green bull and the piebald horse to punish his enemies, will chastise him. So the wily toad is made judge, demands to see the trap first — and while he and the tiger study the matter, the priest runs off inside the monastery gates, and Old Speckled Back, deciding against the tiger, hops into a rock crevice to defy him. Poking his nose inside the crack, the raging tiger rubs it so hard on the rough rock that he bleeds to death.
summary.zh: 江原道有虎曰『山伯』，自詡無傷。遇鏡而撲，陷於阱。僧慈悲，開阱放之。虎曰『謝君，然吾飢，必食君』。樹神、石神皆譴其忘恩。虎猶欲食，乃以蟾蜍為判官。蟾蜍請先視阱，虎急往；僧趁機入寺閉門，蟾蜍判虎負而入石縫以避之。虎怒探鼻於石隙，磨之流血而死。獵者得皮骨而致富，蟾蜍子孫傳其智。

passages.text: On coming round a great rock, Mountain Uncle suddenly saw in his path, as he thought, a big tiger like himself. He stopped, twitched his tail most ferociously as a challenge, showed fight by growling, and got ready to spring. What was his surprise to see the other tiger doing exactly the same things. After a tremendous leap in the air he landed in a pit and all of a heap, bruised and disappointed: the hunter had concealed the pit with sticks and leaves, and on the upright timbers had hung a looking-glass, and the tiger, not seeing any water, was deceived into thinking a real tiger wanted to fight him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Unmannerly Tiger' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by a Buddhist priest came along, who believed in being kind to all living creatures; hearing an animal moaning, he opened the trap and lifting the lid saw old Mountain Uncle at the bottom licking his bruised paw. Thereupon the priest lifted up one of the logs and slid it down until it rested on the bottom of the pit, and the tiger climbed up and out. 'I am deeply grateful to you, sir, for helping me out of my trouble. Nevertheless, as I am very hungry, I must eat you up.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Unmannerly Tiger' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The spirit in the tree spoke through the rustling leaves and declared that the man should go free and that the tiger was both ungrateful and unmannerly. 'The man is certainly right, venerable Mountain Uncle, and you are wholly wrong,' said the spirit in the rock. 'Your master, the Mountain Spirit, who rides on the green bull and the piebald horse to punish his enemies, will certainly chastise you if you devour this priest.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Unmannerly Tiger' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: To be sure of saving his own skin, the priest proposed to make the toad a judge. Old Speckled Back looked as solemn as a magistrate: 'I must go and see the trap before I can make up my mind.' The tiger, moving fast, was there first — which was just what the toad, a friend of the priest, wanted. While the toad and the tiger were studying the matter, the priest ran off and saved himself within the monastery gates; and the toad, deciding against Mountain Uncle, hopped into the rock crevice and defied the tiger. Unable to do any harm, the tiger flew into a passion of rage, and poking his nose inside the crack rubbed it so hard on the rough rock that he soon bled to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Unmannerly Tiger' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

region.en: Kitchen flues under the house floors (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 家宅地下煙道（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Fairy lore from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Tokgabi and His Pranks', eBook #67180

summary.en: Tokgabi is the most mischievous sprite in all Korean fairy-land. He lives in the sooty flues that run under the floors from the kitchen to the chimney hole in the ground, delights in smoke and smut, has no lungs, and his skin and eyes are both fire-proof; he is as black as night, loves nothing that has white in it, and is always afraid of a bit of silver, even a hairpin. His favorite game is to make the iron rice-pot lid dance up and down so it tumbles inside the rice kettle. Yet he is kind to good kitchen maids, washing their dishes for them while they sleep; the king of all the Tokgabis keeps a storehouse of gold and gems and fine clothes for good boys and girls and old people kind to the birds and dumb animals — and all sorts of ugly and troublesome things for bad folks, punishing the stingy by making them poor and miserable. In his menagerie the dragon, bear, tortoise, frog, dog and rabbit are man's friends; the tiger, wild boar, leopard, serpent, toad and cat are messengers to punish naughty folks. Knowing the imp does not like red or shining silver, the Koreans wear dazzling white clothes and silver hairpins to protect themselves from his pranks.
summary.zh: 托孤鬼者，朝鮮妖靈之最黠者也。居於地下煙道之中，喜煙火，不畏熱，膚目皆火不能傷，通體黑如夜，最畏白色與銀。其戲則令飯鍋蓋跳舞落於鍋內。然於勤僕則助其浣滌。托孤鬼之王藏金玉寶物以待善人，蓄醜物以罰惡者；其囿中龍、熊、龜、蛙、犬、兔皆人之友，虎、豹、蛇、蟾、貓則其誅惡之使者。故韓人衣尚白、簪用銀，以辟之。

sensitivity.note: Dokkaebi (goblin) lore retold for children; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Tokgabi is the most mischievous sprite in all Korean fairy-land. He lives in the sooty flues that run under the floors along the whole length of the house, from the kitchen at one end of it to the chimney hole in the ground at the other end. He delights in the smoke and smut, and does not mind fire or flame. He has no lungs, and his skin and eyes are both fire-proof. He is as black as night and loves nothing that has white in it. He is always afraid of a bit of silver, even if it be only a hairpin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Tokgabi and His Pranks' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: His favorite game is to make the iron rice-pot lid dance up and down, so that it tumbles inside the rice kettle and cannot easily be got out again. Although Tokgabi plays so many pranks, he is kind to the kitchen maids: when after a hard day's work one is so tired out that she falls asleep, he helps her to do her hard tasks, washing their dishes and cleaning their tables for good servants. They do say that the king of all the Tokgabis has a storehouse full of gold and gems and fine clothes for good boys and girls, and for old people that are kind to the birds and dumb animals; for bad folks he has all sorts of things that are ugly and troublesome, and he punishes stingy people by making them poor and miserable.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Tokgabi and His Pranks' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In his menagerie the kind creatures that help human beings are the dragon, bear, tortoise, frog, dog and rabbit; the cruel and treacherous creatures are the tiger, wild boar, leopard, serpent, toad and cat, the messengers of the Tokgabi king to punish naughty folks. Knowing that the imp does not like red, a young man when betrothed wears clothes of this bright color; Tokgabi is afraid of shining silver too, so the men fasten their topknots together with silver hairpins, and every one who can afford them uses white metal dishes and dresses in snowy garments, to protect themselves from the pranks of Tokgabi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Tokgabi and His Pranks' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: East Light and the Bridge of Fishes

region.en: River below the Dragon's Pool, Paektu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 長白龍淵下流（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Children's retelling of the Chumong cycle from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'East Light and the Bridge of Fishes', eBook #67180

summary.en: A king's servant girl watches the peak that holds the Dragon's Pool and hopes for a son to rule the river country; a tiny bit of shining vapor flies into the bosom of her dress, and she bears a beautiful boy. The jealous king throws the baby among the pigs — the sows breathe into his nostrils; among the horses — the mares warm and nurse him. Bowed by Heaven's will, the king allows the child in the palace, and the youth becomes Master of the Royal Stables, named East Light, Radiance of the Morning, Child of the Sun and Grandson of the Yellow River. When the king grows jealous of his archery, East Light flees with three followers to a great deep river, cries out that the Child of the Sun shall not be stopped, and shoots his arrows into the water: the fish crowd together, and on their spines a bridge is formed over which the four men flee while the bridge dissolves behind them. Three strangers in seaweed, hemp and embroidered robes, representing fishermen-hunters, farmers-artisans and rulers, invite him to be their king; he teaches the people of Fuyu ruler-and-ruled, marriage, cooking, house-building and the topknot, and hundreds of years after his death the tribes south of the Everlasting White Mountains name their country Cho-sen, Morning Radiance, after him.
summary.zh: 侍女望龍淵而禱子，東來一片祥雲入懷，遂孕。王妒，棄兒於豕牢，豕乳之；又棄於馬廄，馬哺乳之。王懼天，乃聽其母子入宮。兒長善騎射，號東明，為王馬奴。王忌其能，東明與三友南奔，至大河無舟，乃彎弓射水，群魚負背成橋而渡。至南地，遇草衣、麻衣、繡衣三人，奉為王，國曰夫餘。東明教民嫁娶、築屋、椎髻。數百年後，南諸部合為一國，取其名曰朝鮮（晨曦之國）。

sensitivity.note: Chumong (Jumong) cycle retold; cf. records jumong-founder and korean-jumong-fish-turtle-bridge — this is the children's recension.

passages.text: One day while watching the mountain top she saw coming from the east a tiny bit of shining vapor. Floating like a white cloud in the blue sky it seemed no bigger than an egg. It came nearer and nearer until it seemed to go into the bosom of her dress. Very soon she became the mother of a boy. It was indeed a most beautiful child. But the jealous king was angry: he took the baby and threw it down among the pigs in the pen — but no, the sows breathed into the baby's nostrils and their warm breath made it live.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'East Light and the Bridge of Fishes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the king heard of this wonderful behavior of pigs and horses, he bowed his head toward Heaven; it seemed the will of the Great One in the Sky that the boy baby should live and grow up to be a man. So he allowed her to bring her child into the palace, where he grew up trained like one of the king's sons, skilful in riding and archery, always kind to animals. The king named the youthful archer and horseman East Light, Radiance of the Morning, and made him Master of the Royal Stables; the people called him Child of the Sun and Grandson of the Yellow River.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'East Light and the Bridge of Fishes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Fearing he might lose his life if he remained near the king, East Light with three trusty followers fled southward until he came to a great, deep river, wide and impassable, with his enemies swiftly pursuing. In a great strait he cried out, 'Alas, shall I, the Child of the Sun and the Grandson of the Yellow River, be stopped here powerless by this stream?' Then as if his father, the Sun, had whispered to him what to do, he drew his bow and shot many arrows here and there into the water. The waters appeared strangely agitated; the fish crowded together in so dense a mass that on their spines a bridge was soon formed, on which men could stand. Over the bridge of fish backs, scaly and full of spiny fins, the four young men fled; as soon as they gained the opposite shore the bridge of fishes dissolved, and scarcely had they swum away when the pursuers gained the water's edge — the shafts fell short and the river was too deep and wide to swim their horses over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'East Light and the Bridge of Fishes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: East Light met three strange persons who seemed to be awaiting his coming: the first dressed in seaweed, the second in hempen garments, and the third in embroidered robes — representing the three classes of society, fishermen and hunters, farmers and artisans, and rulers of the tribes. They welcomed him warmly and invited him to be their king. In the land named Fuyu, rich in the five grains, the new king ruled long and happily, teaching the proper relations of ruler and ruled, the laws of marriage, better methods of cooking and house-building, and the wearing of the topknot. Hundreds of years after East Light died, the tribes and states in the peninsula south of the Everlasting White Mountains, wanting to become one nation and one kingdom, called their country after East Light in a more poetical form — Cho-sen, Morning Radiance, the Land of the Morning Calm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'East Light and the Bridge of Fishes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Prince Sandalwood and the First Topknot

region.en: Sandalwood tree, Mt. Tabak, P'yongyang (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Children's Dangun cycle from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Prince Sandalwood, the Father of Korea', eBook #67180

summary.en: A bear and a tiger on the southern slope of Old Whitehead Mountain, not satisfied with the quality of human beings already on the earth, agree to go before Hananim, the Great One of Heaven and Earth, to ask that their form and nature be changed. A Voice speaks: 'Eat a bunch of garlic and stay in a cave for twenty-one days.' The tiger quits on the eleventh day; the bear waits out the twenty-one, her hairy hide and claws dropping off like an overcoat, and she stands upright a perfect woman beside a brook. Meanwhile Whanung, the Son of the Great One in the Heavens, asks for an earthly kingdom and is given the Land of the Dragon's Back — for our country rose on the first morning of creation out of the sea in the form of a dragon, whose spine is the mountain backbone and whose head is the Ever-White Mountain with the Dragon's Pool on its summit. He descends in a cloud of many colors, finds the bear-woman by the brookside, chooses her as his bride, and a baby boy is born, reared in a cradle of soft moss. The people under the sandalwood tree on Mt. Tabak see the cloud stand over the sacred tree, and a white-robed youth of grand and august appearance alights: 'I have come from my ancestors in Heaven to rule over you, my children.' They salute him the August and Venerable Sandalwood; he teaches why the bear is good and the tiger bad, ordains the topknot for married men and the braid for boys, the pagoda hairdo of women at marriage — 'Thus our Korean civilization was begun, and to this day the law of the hat and hair distinguishes us above all people.'
summary.zh: 熊與虎同詣天帝（漢拏）乞化人身。神諭曰『食蒜，居洞二十一日則化』。虎十一日而出；熊忍至二十一日，毛皮自脫，化為絕色女子，坐於溪畔。時天帝之子桓雄求下界治國，遂賜龍脊之地（朝鮮也——大地初闢之日自海湧出如龍，其脊為山脈，其首即白頭山龍淵）。桓雄降於彩雲之中，遇熊女而聘之，生子於苔蘚之搖籃。民見雲停檀樹之上，中有白衣神人，肅然曰『吾奉天命來治爾民』。眾拜曰檀聖。乃教民束髮為髻、婚嫁之禮，又授以熊善虎惡之訓。我國文明自此而始。

sensitivity.note: Dangun children's recension; parallel records dangun, korean-dangun-wanggeom, korean-dangun-sandal-prince-variant.

passages.text: Long, long ago, before there were any refined people in the Land of Dawn, a bear and a tiger met together on the southern slope of Old Whitehead Mountain in the forest. These wild animals were not satisfied with the kind of human beings already on the earth, and they wanted better ones: they agreed to go before Hananim, the Great One of Heaven and Earth, and ask him to change at once their form and nature. Then a Voice spoke out saying, 'Eat a bunch of garlic and stay in a cave for twenty-one days. If you do, you will become human.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Prince Sandalwood' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was cold and gloomy in the cave, and finally on the eleventh day the tiger, seeing no signs of losing his stripes, concluded to give up and bounded out of the cave to go hunting in the woods. But the bear, patiently sucking her paw, waited till the twenty-one days had passed. Then her hairy hide and claws dropped off, like an overcoat. Her nose and ears suddenly shortened and she stood upright — a perfect woman. Walking out of the cave the new creature sat beside a brook, and in the pure water beheld how lovely she was.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Prince Sandalwood' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Whanung, the Son of the Great One in the Heavens, asked his father to give him an earthly kingdom to rule over, and the Lord of Heaven presented his son with the Land of the Dragon's Back, which men called Korea. This country rose up on the first morning of creation out of the sea in the form of a dragon; his spine, loins and tail form the great range of mountains that makes the backbone of our beautiful country, while his head rises skyward in the eternal White Mountain in the North, on whose summit lies the blue lake of pure water, the Dragon's Pool. Down out of his cloud of many colors Whanung descended first to the mountain top and then to the lower earth, where he found a beautiful woman sitting by the brookside — the bear that had been transformed into lovely human shape and nature. He chose her as his bride, and by and by a little baby boy was born, whom the mother made a cradle of soft moss and reared in the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Prince Sandalwood' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The people who dwelt at the foot of the mountain saw the cloud move southward until it stood over the sacred sandalwood tree on a small mountain named Tabak, when out stepped a white-robed being who alighted in the forest. There sat under the tree a youth of grand appearance, arrayed in princely dress; despite his youth, he was wise and venerable. 'I have come from my ancestors in Heaven to rule over you, my children.' At once the people fell on their knees: 'Thou art our king, we acknowledge thee.' Seeing that the people were rough and unkempt, Prince Sandalwood showed them how to tie up and dress their hair: men should wear their long locks in the form of a topknot, boys must braid their hair and let it hang down their backs, and women must plait their tresses plainly at the neck, except at marriage or on great occasions, when they might pile up their hair like a pagoda. Thus our Korean civilization was begun, and to this day the law of the hat and hair distinguishes us above all people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Prince Sandalwood' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rabbit's Crystal Eyes in the Sea-Palace

region.en: Palace of the fish-king under the waves (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Animal trickster tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Rabbit's Eyes', eBook #67180

summary.en: Every creature with fins and a tail is in distress, for the king of the fishes has a fishhook stuck fast in his gills, giving him fever and much pain. All the wise creatures are summoned, and Dr. Turtle, most learned of them all, decides that nothing less than a poultice made of rabbits' eyes will loosen the hook. Ordered to invite a rabbit down under the sea, the turtle dazzles Brother Bunny with tales of gems and jewels, golden trees and music in the world under the waves, and carries him down on his shell. While the rabbit enjoys the palace honors, he overhears the doctors and learns why he was brought there; told politely by the royal executioners that he must give up his eyes, he regrets 'that the eyes I have in my head now are not real eyes, but only crystal — I was afraid that sea water would hurt my sight, so I took out my ordinary eyes, buried them in the sand and put on these crystal ones.' If allowed to return to the beach he will dig them up. Getting on the turtle's back, Brother Bunny jumps off in a jiffy, scampers to the woods, and shows only his cotton tail; Dr. Turtle sheds tears and returns to tell how a rabbit had outwitted him.
summary.zh: 魚王喉中著鉤，百醫無策。龜大夫曰『非兔眼膏莫治』，乃上山以海底之富誘兔。兔欣然乘龜背入海，遊於龍宮。既而聞醫者議取其目，兔詭言『今所用者水晶目也，真目已埋於沙，懼海水傷之也；容吾返岸取之』。遂乘龜背出水上，一躥入林，惟見白尾。龜大夫垂淚而歸。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Dragon-Palace rabbit tale (cf. korean-rabbit-turtle-eyes); no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There was trouble down in the fish world under the waves: the king of the fishes was suffering with a dreadful pain in his mouth, for while swimming around outside his palace he gulped down what looked good to eat and found he had barely escaped swallowing a fish hook, which stuck fast in his gills. All the wise creatures in the ocean were summoned to the palace, and the turtle, considered the most learned and expert of them all, finally decided that nothing less than a poultice made of rabbits' eyes would loosen the hook and end His Majesty's troubles.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Rabbit's Eyes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Dr. Turtle was ordered to go to the seashore and invite a rabbit to come down into the world under the sea. He dazzled Brother Bunny with tales of most wonderful mountains and valleys on the floor of the deep sea, with rare water plants, trees of gold and silver, flowers of every color, good things to eat and drink, music and dancing, handsome serving maids. 'Come along and be our guest. Our king has sent me to invite you.' Down, down below the blue waves they sank until they arrived at the king's palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Rabbit's Eyes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: While Mr. Rabbit was enjoying himself he overheard them talking, and found out why they had brought him there and shown him such honors. Horrified at the idea of losing his eyes, he determined to save his sight and play the tortoise a smart trick. When politely informed by the royal executioners that he must give up his eyes to make the king well, Brother Bunny broke out with equally polite regrets: 'Really I am so sorry that His Majesty is ill, but the eyes I have in my head now are not real eyes, but only crystal. I was afraid that sea water would hurt my sight, so I took out my ordinary eyes, buried them in the sand and put on these crystal ones, which I usually wear in very dusty or wet weather. If you will allow me to return to the beach, I'll dig them up and return in time for the poultice-making.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Rabbit's Eyes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: So, getting on Dr. Turtle's back, Brother Bunny was soon out of the water and on land. In a jiffy he jumped off, scampered away, and reached the woods, showing only his cotton tail; soon he was out of sight. Dr. Turtle shed tears and returned to tell how a rabbit had outwitted him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Rabbit's Eyes' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

texts.period: Kija legend retold in Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Topknots and Crockery Hats', eBook #67180

summary.en: Long before Confucius was born, the wise Kija, chief counselor at court, refuses to serve the new dynasty, and emigrates eastward with five thousand of the best people to teach the savage people manners and refinement. Over the plains of Manchuria they march toward the rising sun, cross the Duck Green River (the Yalu) and come to the Great Eastern River, where the land is beautiful; from the tinted clouds at sunrise the new country has been named Cho-sen, Land of Morning Radiance. He builds the boat-shaped capital Ping Yang — within its walls no wells shall be dug lest the boat sink, and a rock pillar to the west to which the boat city shall be forever moored. With his wise men he publishes eight great laws, lays out roads and measures, and teaches the flue-warmed house. To stop the street fights of a rough people, he republishes the law of Dan Kun and establishes the topknot; and when the topknot becomes a handle for brawlers, he invents hats of baked clay four feet across and two feet high, weighing many pounds, so that quarrels become a silent battle of ugly faces — 'a noiseless duel, or a quarrel between deaf and dumb folks' — until a gentleness like a great calm settles over the land. The women get the clubs, changed from skull-crackers into starch polishers, and ruffians become gentlemen.
summary.zh: 箕子不忍事新朝，率五千良民東遷，渡鴨綠江，都平壤。城形如舟，城中不鑿井，恐舟沉也；城西立石柱，以為繫舟之樁。頒八條之律，教民掘地為炕以暖室。俗悍好鬥，乃復檀君束髮之令，定男子結髻、未婚者辮髮之制。鬥者揪髻，乃命陶工製陶冠，徑四尺、高逾二尺，戴者相鬥惟碎其冠，損則自償，費半歲之資。於是鬥毆化為瞪目切齒之啞戰，久而民風漸馴。碎顱之棒改為擣衣之杵，悍夫化為君子。

sensitivity.note: Kija founding legend retold; parallel korean-kija-colonization-choson (Hulbert version).

passages.text: Long, long ago in China, even centuries before the great Confucius was born, there lived a wise and learned man named Kija, the chief counselor at court. When a great war broke out and a new line of rulers came into power, Kija declined to serve the king of the country and resolved to emigrate to the far East, to teach the savage people manners and refinement. The new king allowed five thousand of the best people, most of them Kija's followers, to accompany their master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Topknots and Crockery Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: They crossed the Duck Green River, which we call the Yalu, and came to the Great Eastern River, where the land was very beautiful; from the tinted clouds at sunrise the new country had been named Cho-sen, or Land of Morning Radiance. Having laid out a city for his colony, Kija began to build a wall, naming the city Ping Yang, Northern Castle. 'Now that we have safely arrived as after a voyage, the city shall be shaped like a boat. Within its walls no wells shall be dug, lest this, like boring holes, should make the boat sink; on the outside, to the west, shall stand the rock pillar to which the boat city shall be forever moored.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Topknots and Crockery Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kija was ably assisted by his wise men, who published eight great laws for the kingdom, laid out roads, established measures and distances, and taught the people how to build houses with a kang, warmed by flues running under the floors. The people were rough and savage and constantly given to hard fighting; so Kija republished the law of Dan Kun, the spirit of the mountain, and ordered that every married man should bind up his hair into a knot on top of his head, while the younger fellows must plait their hair in a braid down their backs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Topknots and Crockery Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nevertheless the rough people used the topknot as a handle to catch hold of when fighting in the streets. To stop these quarrels, Kija caused big heavy hats to be moulded of clay, four feet across and two feet high, weighing many pounds, baked in ovens until hard as stone. Every fellow who was known to quarrel was compelled to wear one; when men fought they only cracked their crockery, and a good half year's wages was required to pay for a new hat. Before many months a street quarrel got to be a perfectly silent battle of ugly faces and terrible gestures; in time a gentleness like a great calm settled over the land. The clubs of the rough men were handed over to the wives and daughters for pounding and starching clothes, and thus by changing sticks that had been used as skull-crackers into starch polishers, Kija changed also ruffians into gentlemen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Topknots and Crockery Hats' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Fancha, the Heaven-Born and the Sacred Magpie

region.en: Lake of Heaven beyond the Ever-White Mountains (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Ancestor-legend of the Manchus retold by Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Fancha and the Magpie', eBook #67180

summary.en: When the Manchu conquerors sit on the thrones of China in satin and jeweled robes, they want to know who their ancestors were, and the Emperor summons the 117-year-old Mrs. Crinkles. On the other side of the Ever White Mountains is the Land of Lakes, whose crystal flood reflects the snow-covered mountains and is spangled with jewels at night; three lovely virgins of the Heavenly palaces descend with the Lord of Heaven's permission to bathe in it, choosing the magpie as their sacred bird. One day a magpie flies down bearing a blood-red fruit and drops it on the garment of the youngest sister; the gift is a happy omen, and from this divine token the youngest conceives and bears a son, Golden Family Stem, who will found a dynasty named Great Bright. Growing up under mountains that seem to touch the sky, he loses his mother, takes the name Fancha, Heaven-born, builds a boat and floats down the river to three tribes at war; his noble appearance and fearless arrival win the shout 'Our chief!' He builds a city, marries a princess — and when war kills him and all his sons but one, that son, pursued into a dark wood, is delivered by the sacred magpie that settles on his head: the pursuers take the still figure for a dried wood splinter and rush past. 'The rest of the story Your Majesty knows, for Fancha was your ancestor of seventeen generations ago.'
summary.zh: 滿洲既入主中國，欲知其祖之所自出。乃召百十七歲之嫗入宮述古。白山之外有鏡湖，三天女奉旨降浴於湖，以鵲為神鳥。一日鵲啣朱果置幼女衣上，女吞之而孕，生子曰『金族之幹』，將啟『大明』之基。孤兒長，自號『天生者』，乘舟而下，三族奉為酋長。傳至戰歿，惟一子逃於密林，神鵲集其首，追者以為枯木而過之。嫗曰：『此即陛下十七世之祖也。』帝厚賚之。

sensitivity.note: Manchu Three Fairies of Tianchi founding myth as told in a Korean children's book; cross-border origin narrative.

passages.text: On the other side of the Ever White Mountains, which divide Korea from Manchuria, is the Land of Lakes. On one of these, as in a mirror, the glorious blue sky and the snow-covered mountains are reflected, and at night when the stars come out the waveless mirror is spangled with jewels. There were three lovely virgins who dwelt in the Heavenly palaces and they wanted to come down and bathe in the water of this lake; permission was given them by the Lord of Heaven, and descending to the earth they were as happy as fairies could be, choosing the magpie as their sacred bird.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Fancha and the Magpie' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day they noticed a magpie flying far above them, which bore in its bill a blood-red fruit. Descending near where their clothes lay on the beach, it dropped the red fruit on the garment of the youngest of the sisters. They agreed that this gift of the bird, which was sacred in their eyes, was a happy omen; from this divine token brought by a magpie, the youngest of the virgins conceived and bore a son. They named the baby boy Golden Family Stem, for they felt sure that he would grow up and become the founder of a dynasty of kings, who should take the name of Great Bright from the shining water near which he was born.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Fancha and the Magpie' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by his dear mother's breath ceased and she entered into the icy caves of the dead, and he found himself an orphan; he resolved to take the name of Fancha, or Heaven-born, and to go out into the world and lead men. He built a boat and floated down the outlet of the lake into a river, landing at a place where three tribes or clans were at war. When they saw this noble youth alone and unarmed step fearlessly over the gunwale of the boat, they were mightily impressed, and when he told the story of his birth they one and all shouted 'Our chief!' In time he built a city, and for his wife and queen married a princess of the principal tribe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Fancha and the Magpie' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In one of the battles he and all his sons except one were killed. This one, named Fancha, was chased by the enemy over the open plains; but when he reached a dense dark wood a deliverer came to him in the form of the sacred bird, the magpie, which settled on his head. He stood as still as a post, and the pursuers, seeing the bird, supposed the figure was a piece of dried wood or the splinter of a tree struck by lightning, and rushed on and past him. 'The rest of the story Your Majesty knows, for Fancha was your ancestor of seventeen generations ago' — and the great Emperor of all the Chinas loaded the aged woman with presents and honors, creating for her the office of Chief Story-Teller to the Imperial children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Fancha and the Magpie' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sneezing Colossus and the Pear

region.en: Mountain miryek, colossal stone Buddha (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Fairy tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The Sneezing Colossus', eBook #67180

summary.en: Lazy Mr. Kim, scolded by his wife to find something for the household, rambles over the rocks until noon, when he comes to one of the mighty mir-yeks, colossal stone Buddhas cut out of the solid mountain in the days when monasteries covered the land. Out of a crevice in the head grows a pear tree, and at the end of the outer branch a ripe pear nearly as big as a man's head. Seizing the vines he climbs to the chin, but the polished nose is slippery and the ears too smooth; so he crawls up into the right nostril — and suddenly a blast loud enough to rend the mountain: the colossus has sneezed, and got rid of the intruder. Mr. Kim flies through the air and lies unconscious till near sundown; in sneezing so hard the colossus has shaken its head, and the big pear has dropped off — Kim finds it lying by his side, and goes home rejoicing to a merry supper with his little dog.
summary.zh: 懶漢金氏奉妻命入山覓食，至山中石佛（彌勒）之前。佛首裂罅生梨樹，枝頭一梨大如人首。金攀藤至佛頷，鼻滑不可登，遂自鼻孔而入。忽聞巨響，石佛打嚏，噴之出，拋於荊棘之間，昏至日昃。梨亦因佛搖首而墜，適在其側。金攜歸，與犬共食，大快。

sensitivity.note: Comic legend of a Buddha image; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Mr. Kim went out to the mountains to find something. He came to one of the mighty mir-yeks, or colossal stone Buddhas, cut out of the solid mountain. Ages ago in the days of Buddhism, when monasteries covered the land, devout men, laboring many months, chiseled this towering colossus into human form: its nose stood out three feet, its mouth was four feet wide, and on its flat head was a cap of granite on which ten men could stand. But out of a crevice in the head of the figure grew a pear tree, and, oh joy! at the end of the outer branch was growing a ripe, luscious pear nearly as big as a man's head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sneezing Colossus' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seizing hold of the bushes and wild grape-vines, Mr. Kim climbed upward and got as far as the chin of the great stone face. The nose, being polished, was slippery and the ears were too smooth to climb. A bright thought entered his head: he would crawl up into the right nostril and hope for an exit to the top, and soon the man Kim disappeared from sight as with hands and feet he climbed into the darkness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sneezing Colossus' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suddenly a blast loud enough to rend the mountain was heard. Hash-ho! No, the colossus had sneezed. Thus the stone man got rid of the intruder. The first thing Mr. Kim knew, he was flying through the air, and he tumbled upon the bushes. Mr. Kim lay asleep or unconscious till near sun-down; but in sneezing so hard, the colossus had shaken its head also and the big pear had dropped off. Kim found it lying by his side, and picking it up went on his way rejoicing; at home the little dog barked welcome, and a right merry supper they had over the big pear cut into slices.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The Sneezing Colossus' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

region.en: Underground by the river Kingin's stone colossus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 金因江畔石佛之下（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Animal courtship tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole', eBook #67180

summary.en: By the river Kingin stands the great stone image cut out of solid rock; down under the earth near it lives a mole whose daughter is the most wonderful mole baby ever known, and Father Mole determines she shall marry only the grandest thing in the universe. The wise ones agree the Great Blue Sky is above everything; but the Sky refers him to the Sun, who controls it; the Sun confesses the Cloud is greater, able to cover him for days and weeks; the Cloud, inky black with storm, laughs and refers him to the Wind; the Wind confesses that before Miryek, the colossal stone image, his power is naught — smite him as he may, the stone stands unmoved and smiling. So the footsore Mole Father proceeds to Miryek, which grants that it fears not sky, sun, frost, clouds, lightning or thunder — 'Yes, I am great. But I am not the greatest: down under my feet is the Mole. His might I cannot resist; soon he shall undermine my base and I shall topple down. By universal confession, the Mole is the greatest thing in the universe, and to him I yield. Better marry your daughter to him.' The daughter's bridegroom is found at home, of the same family of creatures, and great is the joy at the wedding.
summary.zh: 鼴父欲以女嫁天下至尊者。問於智者，皆曰天也。天曰『日能主我』；日曰『雲能蔽我』；雲曰『風能驅我』；風曰『石佛之前，吾力為虛，吾吼之而彼不瞬』。遂謁石佛。佛曰：『誠然，吾不畏天，不畏日，不畏霜雪雷霆。然吾足之下有鼴焉，其力吾不能抗，日掘吾基，吾必傾覆。以天下之大，莫大於鼴。可以女妻鼴。』鼴父乃歸，嫁女於同族之美少年，閤家大喜。

passages.text: By the river Kingin stands the great stone image, or Miryek, that was cut out of the solid rock ages ago. Down under the earth near this mighty colossus lived a soft-furred mole and his wife. One day a daughter was born to them, the most wonderful mole baby that ever was known. Father Mole determined to marry her only to the grandest thing in the whole universe, and the wise ones agreed that the Great Blue Sky was above everything else in glory and greatness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'No, I am not the greatest,' said the Sky; 'I must refer you to the Sun. He controls me, for he can make it day or night as he pleases.' The mighty luminary seemed suddenly very modest: 'Alas! I am not master. The Cloud is greater than I, for he is able to cover me up and make me invisible for days and weeks.' The Cloud, its face inky black with the wrath of a storm, almost laughed: 'So far from being the greatest thing in the world, I am not even my own master. See already how the wind is driving me. Let me commend you to the Wind.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Wind was not half so proud as the Mole Father had expected, and confessed that before Miryek, the colossal stone image, his power was naught. 'I smite that Great Stone Face and its eyes do not even blink. I roar in his ears, but he minds it not. I try to make him sneeze, but he will not. Alas, no. I am not the grandest thing in the universe, while Miryek stands. Go to him.' Miryek granted with stony patience: 'I care not for the sky day or night. I fear not the sun, that cannot melt me, nor the frost that is not able to make me crumble. The clouds come and go, but they cannot move me. Yes, I am great.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I would gladly do so, if I were greatest. But I am not,' said Miryek. 'Down under my feet is the Mole. He digs with his shovel-like hands and makes burrows day and night. His might I cannot resist. Soon he shall undermine my base and I shall topple down and lie like common stone along the earth. Yes! by universal confession, the Mole is the greatest thing in the universe and to him I yield. Better marry your daughter to him.' So after all his journeying the father sought no further; he found his daughter's bridegroom at home and of the same family of creatures, and great was the joy and rejoicing at the wedding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'A Bridegroom for Miss Mole' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Old White Whiskers and the Ring of Dry Grass

region.en: Icy river crossing, Kang-wen mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 江原道冰河（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Animal trickster tale from Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'Old White Whiskers and Mr. Bunny', eBook #67180

summary.en: White Whiskers is the proudest tiger in the peninsula, retainer of the great genii of the mountains — the Mountain Spirit, when he wants to, can call together all the tigers in his domain and ride off on the clouds astride the biggest. White Whiskers' business is to visit the hill-pass shrines daily and see that offerings continue; the people offer sacrifice out of fear of the Mountain Spirit and his servants. Yet proud as he is, he is outwitted by a creature without strength or sting. Crossing the ice one cold winter's day, Mr. Rabbit meets him face to face, and offers a royal dinner: lie down on the ice, shut your eyes, and I will circle you with dry grass, driving the game to your very paws — 'don't open your eyes till I give you the word.' As quickly as one can blow out a candle the tiger is asleep; Mr. Bunny piles a thick ring of combustibles around him, sets it on fire, and watches. Awakened by the crackling, the tiger has to jump high to escape with his life, one paw scorched so that he limps and his fur singed so that all his long hair and fine looks are gone; the other tigers laugh at him, and the great Mountain Spirit no longer trusts such a stupid servant.
summary.zh: 白鬚虎者，山神之爪牙也，最驕。冬日冰上遇兔，兔曰『吾為王驅獸至爪下，王閉目臥於冰，吾以枯草環之』。虎喜而寢。兔積草成環，縱火焚之。虎跳而出，爪焦毛燼，威儀盡失。同類笑之，山神亦不復信用。

passages.text: White Whiskers was the name of a huge, tawny tiger that lived in the mountains of Kang Wen, the proudest tiger in the whole peninsula of Korea. He was the retainer of the great genii of the mountains, that men feared and worshiped; the Mountain Spirit, when he wanted to, could call together all the tigers in his domain, and sitting astride the back of the biggest, ride off on the clouds or to victory over Korea's enemies. One particular matter of business confided to White Whiskers was to visit daily the shrines in the hill passes to see if offerings were continually made.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old White Whiskers and Mr. Bunny' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Just as he was crossing a river on the ice, Mr. Bunny met Old White Whiskers face to face, and knew his last hour had come. 'Oh, why should you bother with me? I'm so little and skinny as hardly to make a mouthful for Your Majesty. Just listen to me and I'll get you a royal dinner. I'll go up the mountain and drive the game to your very paws. Only you must do exactly what I tell you: lie down on the ice here, shut your eyes and do not stir. If you hear a noise and even some crackling, don't open your eyes till I give you the word.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old White Whiskers and Mr. Bunny' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old White Whiskers, both hungry and tired, resolved while waiting to take a good nap; as quickly as one can blow out a candle, he was asleep. Mr. Bunny made himself busy pulling up all the dry grass he could find and piling it around and close up to Old White Whiskers, then set it on fire. Awakened by the crackling, the tiger had to jump high to escape from the flames with his life; one paw was scorched so that he limped, and his fur was singed so badly that all his long hair and fine looks were gone. When he got back home the other tigers laughed at him; henceforth he had to take second place, for the great Mountain Spirit no longer trusted such a stupid servant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'Old White Whiskers and Mr. Bunny' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

title.en: King Peony and the Cinnamon Rose

texts.period: Parable told by the scholar Sul Chong to King Sinmun of Silla; retold in Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales (c. 1913), 'The King of the Flowers', eBook #67180

summary.en: Twelve centuries ago lived Sul Chong, the greatest of all the learned men of Korea, and when the King of Silla, Sin Mun, was living in luxury and filling his palace with too many pretty dancing girls, Sul Chong warned his master with a story: in spring the Peony, king of the flowers, blossomed so gorgeously that hundreds made long journeys to see him, and a single peony on one stem was saluted as king of the whole garden. All the flowers trooped to the floral court — Peach, Plum, Pear, Apple and Persimmon, then the virgin flowers, Tea-Rose, Azalea, Lily, Strawberry Blossom, and last of all the Cinnamon Rose, tripping along in a green skirt and red jacket with haughty air and breath of spice. King Peony lingers long with the spicy visitor, invites her to the palace, and leaves his ministers to carry on the government — Miss Cinnamon Rose seems the real ruler. But one day there comes the flower called Old Man, like an aged beggar in sackcloth: 'If you keep company with the wise and prudent, your reign will be long, powerful and glorious; but if you consort with the foolish your house will fall. Did not three dynasties of the emperors of Great China fall because of the beautiful women who tempted their Majesties to forget their duties?' The king blushes to a deep crimson, confesses his faults and reforms his life — and it is said the lesson was not lost on the real human king, who dismissed his harem and ruled wisely till the day of his death.
summary.zh: 新羅儒宗薛聰以花國之喻諫王：牡丹為百花之王，百卉來朝，末有薔薇，綠裙紅襖，妖冶善媚。王惑之，日與之處，而政事廢弛。後有『老翁花』者，襤褸如丐，入而諫曰：『近賢則國祚長；近佞則宗廟危。三代之亡，皆以女色。』王大悟，遂黜嬖倖，勵精圖治。此即薔薇所以配伎女、牡丹所以比賢君之故也。

sensitivity.note: Flower-court parable from Silla tradition; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Twelve centuries ago lived the renowned scholar Sul Chong, the greatest of all the learned men of Korea. When the King of Silla, Sin Mun, was living in luxury and filling his palace with too many pretty dancing girls, who distracted his mind from attending properly to the affairs of state, Sul Chong warned his master against the increasing influence of these women by telling him a story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Flowers' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Once upon a time, in spring, the Peony, king of the flowers, blossomed so gorgeously that hundreds of people made long journeys to see the bright blossoms; the king of the whole garden was a single peony grown on one stem, so that all the strength and nourishment of the plant were concentrated in that unique royal bloom. All the other flowers came to pay their respects at the floral court: the Peach, Plum, Pear, Apple and Persimmon trooped in; then the Tea-Rose, the Azalea, the Lily, the Strawberry Blossom; last of all appeared the Cinnamon Rose, tripping nimbly along in a green skirt and red jacket, with haughty air and breath of spice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Flowers' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Of them all, the king seemed most to favor Miss Cinnamon Flower; he invited her to come and live in the palace, and leaving his ministers to carry on the government, spent all his time in her society, so that Miss Cinnamon Rose seemed to be the real ruler instead of the king himself. But one day there came to the palace the flower called Old Man, who looked exactly like an aged beggar dressed in sackcloth and leaning on a staff. 'Although you dress in Chinese silk and none are equal to you in the magnificence of your robes, yet you need a common knife string, as well as I. If you keep company with the wise and prudent, your reign will be long, powerful and glorious; but if you consort with the foolish your house will fall. Did not three dynasties of the emperors of Great China fall because of the beautiful women who tempted their Majesties to forget their duties?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Flowers' (c. 1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king blushed, even to a deep crimson. He confessed his faults and reformed his life. It is said the lesson was not lost on the real human king: he dismissed his harem, sent away the dancing girls and ruled wisely till the day of his death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Korean Fairy Tales, 'The King of the Flowers' (c. 1913); not verbatim.
